citations.review_text: It's Don't Starve, the game in itself is pretty fun, but in the interest of being honest, this version is absolute trash. They updated and updated and updated Dont Starve TOGETHER, SO MANY TIMES, and left this version behind in the dust, to the point where if you've played and gotten used to Dont Starve Together, this version just feels like a slow, trashy, alpha version. Not worth buying, at all, considering you can just buy DST and play offline, alone, and have all the new, nice stuff.

Most of my hours for this game are on my Switch. Riddled with bugs and blurry sprites, but otherwise still a great survival experience despite DST taking over the franchise. I will always believe that Adventure Mode is one of if not the best part of the entirety of Don't Starve, so honestly I could definitely see the appeal of playing this over DST if you're by yourself.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that waiting through the night phase without being able to perform actions hinders the gameplay flow.

citations.review_text:
Don't Starve is basically a survival game where the world wakes up every morning and asks, "How are we going to ruin this guy's day?"

The art style is fantastic, with its creepy hand-drawn look making even the weirdest creatures feel memorable. The world is also packed with things to discover, but exploring too far without preparing is usually a great way to end up dead.

The survival mechanics are simple to understand but surprisingly deep. You need food, resources, shelter, and a plan for dealing with the night. Then winter arrives and suddenly everything you thought you knew becomes useless.

Death can be brutal, but that's part of the fun. Every failed run teaches you something new, and eventually you start feeling like you actually know what you're doing — right before the game finds another way to kill you.

**9/10 — apparently "don't starve" was a suggestion, not a guarantee.**
Waiting for the night to end without being able to do anything doesn't make the progression of the game fun. It has a cute style and unique gameplay but I quickly lost interest.

I think I just don't get Don't Starve. You essentially can't progress without outside resources and I don't see how that is fun or satisfying. The game is purposefully obtuse and lacking in explanation or guidance to the extreme. I've tried to play a few times and it always ends the same way. A wiki open on one monitor and constant failure. That is not fun.

The idea is brilliant. The execution forgets to teach you anything.

I want to love Don't Starve. The concept is excellent, and the first few hours do pull you in. The longer I played, though, the clearer one problem became: the game does not teach you across rounds. Each round should leave you better prepared for the next. Instead, each round teaches you almost nothing, and the result is a loop that feels less like mastery and more like repetition.

Good survival games make failure productive. You die, you learn something specific, and you come back equipped to do better. Frostpunk is a strong example. You fail a few times, but you understand exactly why, and each restart feels like a fresh opportunity rather than a punishment. Don't Starve rarely gives you that. You die, and most of the time you are not sure what you were supposed to do differently, because the game hides the information you would need in order to learn.
The clearest example is food. Hunger is one of your core meters, yet the game makes it almost impossible to understand what any given food does for you. You cannot easily see how much hunger something restores, the number drains too fast to read a clean before and after, and the interface fights you the whole time. So instead of learning a system, you are left guessing. A whole rabbit somehow seems to feed you less than a single carrot, and the game never explains why. That is not depth. That is a withheld stat.

This is the core issue. Don't Starve is not a game you learn by playing. It is a game you learn by reading about somewhere else. There is an important difference between a game that uses a wiki and a game that requires one. Terraria uses a wiki. The game still teaches you its basics, shows you recipes, and gives you readable feedback, and the wiki only helps you optimize. Don't Starve requires a wiki for basic function, because the in-game learning loop is broken. You can sink dozens of hours into it and still feel like you have learned n…

claims.claim: The game features a distinctive Tim Burton-inspired, cartoony, and morbid art style with a unique soundtrack.

citations.review_text: This game is peak and the soundtrack is awesome play it
Addictive art style and gameplay

The charming cartoon art style might suggest a casual experience, but this game is far more complex and demanding than it first appears. Beneath its colorful visuals lies a deep survival game packed with interconnected systems that constantly challenge the player to adapt and plan ahead.
Exploration is easily one of the game's greatest strengths. The world is filled with unique biomes, strange creatures, and useful resources, and discovering how different plants, animals, and materials fit into your survival strategy is consistently rewarding. Every region brings new dangers, and the changing seasons and world events ensure that even experienced players can't become complacent for long.
Unfortunately, the game can also be extremely tedious at times. Gathering basic resources often requires long periods of repetitive clicking, and many crafting recipes demand substantial investments of time and materials. Transporting resources across large distances only adds to the grind. In this regard, the game shares some of the same frustrations as other survival titles where progression can occasionally feel more like a chore than an adventure.
Combat is another area that never fully clicked for me. Encounters are often less engaging than the survival and exploration systems, yet the consequences of failure are severe. Dying can erase hours of hard-earned progress, and while the game does offer ways to mitigate these losses, they often feel either too late in the progression curve or too cumbersome to maintain.
Despite these frustrations, the game excels at creating meaningful survival challenges. Success feels earned, and knowledge gained from previous failures is often more valuable than any item or upgrade. The difficulty strikes a satisfying balance, rewarding preparation, strategy, and experience. Combined with a wide variety of characters, maps, and customization options that encourage different playstyles, the game offers a tremendous amount of replayability for those w…

Open World Survival Crafting Single-Player game with an nice cartoony graphic style. :3

The characters have strengths and weaknesses and some have a aktive ability.

It is very hard to learn how to play, but it is very fun anyways. :3

I recommend it. :3

claims.claim: Combat and crafting systems can feel clunky, with enemies that can easily stun-lock or kill the player and inventory space that is very limited.

citations.review_text:
A deeply unrewarding and frustrating experience. The systems for crafting, equipping, and fighting enemies are not robust and flexible enough to accommodate stun-locking enemies with no clear hitbox that will kill you within 4 hits. Any enemies strong enough to require armor will break it in less than 10, and trying to craft anything while avoiding enemies in combat is a clunky and near-impossible task.
Inventory space is shockingly small, weapons extremely weak, exploration is required yet punishing and extremely bloated by often times requiring a single structure or object on a map to continue, hidden behind massive hordes of extremely powerful enemies that will quickly kill or stun-lock even well-prepared players.
Even with a battery of mods to try and solve these fundamental issues, I unfortunately cannot recommend this game, and regret spending so many hours frustrated while wrestling its endless challenges.

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight the Tim Burton-inspired gothic art style and soundtrack.

citations.review_text: This roguelike is highly addictive. It has a really great Tim Burton-style atmosphere. And there are an enormous number of mods.

A brilliantly punishing experience. If you are looking for a game that challenges your instincts in a flawlessly crafted world, this is an absolute must-have. The very first thing that captures you is the game's amazing art direction. It feels like a Tim Burton sketchbook brought to life. The gothic, sketch-like illustrations make the world feel alive, eerie, and strangely beautiful all at once. If you are diving into the survival genre for the very first time, this is the perfect place to start. Surviving your first harsh winter or managing your sanity meter feels like a massive victory. Every permadeath teaches you a real lesson, making you eager to start a new world immediately. Balancing health, hunger, and creeping madness keeps you on the edge of your seat. Its incredible atmosphere and addictive loop make it unmissable. Don't Starve is an absolute must-have. 10/10

Imagine Tim Burton sitting at a dim bar. Someone sits down next to him and drunkenly starts describing Minecraft (R) to him, and he thinks to himself, "Hey, I could do that."

Welcome to Don't Starve. Victorian gothic atmosphere, quirky art style and musical sound effects, wrapped up into a sometimes hilarious, sometimes terrifying, beautiful little game.
